Day 59 of 100 · Networking Deep Dive

Load Balancing Concepts

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityNetworking Deep DivePublished artifact recovered

Load balancing spreads requests across backends, but availability depends on health semantics, session state and every shared dependency that remains.

Architecture / mental model

client → load balancer → app1 / app2 → shared dependencies

How it works

Round robin distributes requests across available servers, while least-connections selects based on active connections and can better fit workloads with very different request durations.

A process accepting TCP connections is not proof that its database or downstream dependencies are healthy. Passive failure handling and application-level health checks answer different questions.

State stored only in one application process can make users appear logged out when a later request lands on another backend. Stateless applications or shared state stores are usually easier to scale and recover.

Hands-on reference

# Nginx upstream example
upstream app_backend {
  server 10.0.1.10:8000;
  server 10.0.1.11:8000;
}
# Inspect:
curl -I https://example.com
ss -lntp

Verification

Take one backend out of service and observe request behavior. Then test failure of shared dependencies such as database, Redis or the load balancer itself.

Field note / gotcha

Two application servers do not automatically create high availability if one Nginx instance, database, Redis service, network path or availability zone can still stop the service.

Security considerations

Keep backend exposure private, authenticate sensitive health/admin endpoints and avoid putting session or secret data in client routing tricks without understanding the tradeoffs.

What I learned

Load balancing is traffic control, not a spell that makes every dependency immortal.
